content: Tinea capitis is a common fungal infection of the scalp in children, requiring systemic antifungal therapy for effective treatment and to prevent its spread. This updated review evaluates the efficacy of systemic antifungal drugs in children under 18 years of age with confirmed tinea capitis caused by dermatophytes, based on randomized controlled trials (RCTs). In children with Trichophyton infections, terbinafine administered for four weeks and griseofulvin for eight weeks demonstrated similar efficacy in achieving complete clinical and mycological cure. The cure rates were 84.2% for terbinafine and 79.0% for griseofulvin, with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.06 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.98 to 1.15), though the evidence quality was low. Similarly, itraconazole (two to six weeks) and griseofulvin (six weeks) showed comparable cure rates in two studies, with 83.6% and 91.0% respectively (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; very low-quality evidence). No significant differences were observed between itraconazole and terbinafine for two to three weeks of treatment (73.8% versus 78.8%; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.19; low-quality evidence). Fluconazole (two to four weeks) and griseofulvin (six weeks) also showed similar efficacy in three studies, with cure rates of 41.4% and 52.7%, respectively (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; moderate-quality evidence). Evidence comparing ketoconazole and griseofulvin was limited. One study suggested that griseofulvin (12 weeks) was more effective than ketoconazole (12 weeks) for complete cure (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; low-quality evidence). However, when treatment duration was extended to 26 weeks, their efficacy appeared similar (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.07; low-quality evidence). In children with Microsporum infections, a meta-analysis of two studies indicated that griseofulvin (6–12 weeks) was more effective than terbinafine (6 weeks) for complete cure, with cure rates of 50.9% and 34.7%, respectively (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86; moderate-quality evidence). In contrast, terbinafine was more effective than griseofulvin in children with T. tonsurans infections, achieving cure rates of 52.1% versus 35.4% (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.77; moderate-quality evidence). For children with T. violaceum infections, terbinafine and griseofulvin showed similar efficacy (41.3% versus 45.1%; RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.24; low-quality evidence). One study found no significant difference in cure rates between fluconazole administered for three weeks and six weeks in participants with T. tonsurans and M. canis infections (30.2% versus 34.1%; RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.14; low-quality evidence). Additionally, no significant differences were observed between fluconazole and terbinafine (82.0% versus 94.0%; RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.01; low-quality evidence) or between fluconazole and itraconazole (82.0% versus 82.0%; RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.20; low-quality evidence) for complete cure. Adverse events associated with terbinafine, griseofulvin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, and fluconazole were generally mild and reversible. The frequency of adverse events was similar for terbinafine and griseofulvin (9.2% versus 8.3%; RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.57; moderate-quality evidence), and severe adverse events were rare (0.6% for both; RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.24 to 3.88; moderate-quality evidence). Overall, newer antifungal agents such as terbinafine, itraconazole, and fluconazole appear to be at least as effective as griseofulvin for treating Trichophyton infections in children. However, terbinafine may be more effective than griseofulvin for T. tonsurans infections, while griseofulvin may be superior to terbinafine for Microsporum infections. Ketoconazole may be less effective than griseofulvin, though evidence is limited. Most treatments have reasonable safety profiles, and adherence does not appear to differ significantly between shorter courses of terbinafine and longer courses of griseofulvin.
